title: What to watch at the open
text: Stocks ended Friday with a partial bounce. The S&P 500 fund SPY rose 0.3% to $735.29, and the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ rose 1.4% to $656.10. This morning, watch whether the chip makers keep their gains or give some back. A big bounce after a sharp fall does not mean the fall is over. Also watch the 10 year Treasury yield, because high rates have been the main worry for tech stocks.

title: Chip stocks bounced, but they are still far from their highs
text: The five companies that sell parts and equipment for AI (NVIDIA, Broadcom, TSMC, Vertiv, AMD) rose about 4.9% on average on Friday. AMD jumped 11.0% and TSMC 6.3%. The four big AI companies (Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta) were almost flat, up 0.1% on average. Even after the jump, AMD is still about 32% below its 52 week high, and Broadcom is about 41% below its high, close to its 52 week low. One good day does not erase a big drop.

title: Small, risky companies swing the most
text: Rocket Lab jumped 15.4% on Friday, the biggest move on our list, while Intuitive Surgical fell 3.4%. Rocket Lab has a beta of 2.6, which means it tends to move about two and a half times as much as the market. That is why its risk score is the highest on the list (10 out of 10). Big swings can feel exciting when prices go up, but they work the same way on the way down.

title: Rates are still the big worry
text: The 10 year Treasury yield averaged 5.13% in October, up from about 4.06% a year earlier. This yield is what the government pays to borrow money for 10 years. When it is high, safe bonds look more attractive, and fast growing tech stocks can look less attractive. News reports said Friday's strong jobs report pushed yields higher.

title: Lesson 42: Growth stocks and value stocks
text: People often sort stocks into two groups. A growth stock is a company expected to grow fast, so investors pay a high price for it today. They hope the business keeps getting bigger. A value stock looks cheap compared with what the company earns, and it often pays a dividend. Look at our list. AMD has a P/E of about 96, which means investors pay $96 for each $1 of yearly profit. That is a bet on fast growth. Alphabet has a P/E of about 15, which looks more like a value price. Growth stocks can rise a lot, but they usually swing more and can fall harder when interest rates are high. Neither type is better. Many investors own a mix.

title: What this update covers
text: Prices are from Friday's close, November 6, 2026, because the market has not opened yet today.
